Pregnancy

37 to 40 Weeks Pregnant: Full Term and Signs of Labor

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 40 weeks pregnant you have reached your due date: your baby is full term, fully developed, and most people go into labor within a week or two of this point. The stretch from 37 to 40 weeks is a mix of finishing touches for your baby and waiting, watching, and weekly checkups for you. This guide covers what the term labels actually mean, how you might feel, what appointments look like now, and the clear signs that it is time to call or go in.

Early term, full term, and why the labels matter

For years, anything past 37 weeks was casually called full term. The definitions used by ACOG are now more precise, because those extra days matter. Early term runs from 37 weeks 0 days to 38 weeks 6 days. Full term runs from 39 weeks 0 days to 40 weeks 6 days. Late term covers the week after your due date, and post term begins at 42 weeks. Babies born at 39 weeks or later tend to have an easier start with breathing and feeding than babies born in the early term window, which is why elective deliveries are usually not scheduled before 39 weeks without a medical reason.

These labels also shape what happens if your due date passes. Going a few days past 40 weeks is common and, on its own, not an emergency. Most clinicians start talking about closer monitoring and about induction around 41 weeks, and a separate guide on this site walks through that conversation in detail. For now, the useful takeaway is simple: your due date is the middle of a window, not a deadline. A first baby in particular often arrives after the date on the calendar, and that alone says nothing about how labor will go.

How big your baby is now

By 40 weeks, most babies measure about 48 to 52 cm from head to heel and weigh somewhere between 3 and 3.6 kg, roughly 6.5 to 8 pounds. Those are averages, and healthy newborns land on both sides of them. In these final weeks your baby is mostly gaining fat, which smooths the skin, helps regulate temperature after birth, and adds those newborn rolls. The fine hair called lanugo has largely disappeared, and the waxy coating called vernix is shedding into the amniotic fluid, though some babies still arrive with patches of it.

The lungs and brain keep maturing right up to birth, which is part of why the 39 week mark matters. Your baby has also settled into a birth position, usually head down, and has less room to move, but movement should not become weak or infrequent. You should keep feeling the same pattern of rolls, stretches, and pushes you know, right through labor itself. If movements slow down or feel different from your baby's usual pattern, do not wait for the next appointment or until morning. Call your maternity unit or clinician right away, at any hour, because a fresh check is quick and reassuring.

How you might feel from 37 weeks on

Many people feel the baby drop lower into the pelvis in these weeks, especially with a first pregnancy. Breathing may get easier while walking, sleeping, and bathroom trips get harder. Pelvic pressure, hip ache, swollen feet, and sharp little zings in the cervix, sometimes called lightning pain, are all common. You may lose the mucus plug, a thick glob of discharge that can be clear, pink, or streaked with blood. That is a sign the cervix is changing, but labor can still be hours or weeks away. Practice contractions may also get stronger and more frequent without settling into a pattern.

Sleep often falls apart at exactly the moment everyone tells you to rest up. Try a pillow between your knees and one under your bump, small evening meals to calm heartburn, and permission to nap in fragments instead of chasing one long night. The impatience is real too, and worth naming kindly. Watching your due date approach, fielding daily is the baby here yet messages, and inspecting every twinge with suspicion is genuinely tiring. It can help to plan one small pleasant thing per day, mute the check-in texts for a while, and remind yourself that your body does not owe anyone a schedule.

What appointments look like now

From around 36 or 37 weeks, prenatal visits usually move to once a week. Expect the routine basics: blood pressure, a urine check, your baby's heartbeat, and a measure or feel of your belly to confirm growth and position. Your clinician may offer a vaginal exam to see whether the cervix has started to soften, thin, or open. These checks are optional in a routine pregnancy and do not predict when labor will start, so it is fine to accept them or to decline. If you have not yet reviewed your group B strep result and what it means for labor, this is a good week to ask.

Near or past your due date, your clinician may mention a membrane sweep. During a vaginal exam, they sweep a finger around the inside of the cervix to separate the membranes from its edge, which releases natural prostaglandins and can nudge labor to start within a few days. It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous for most people, can cause spotting and cramping afterward, and is always your choice. If you pass 40 to 41 weeks, expect a plan for extra monitoring, often a nonstress test to watch the heartbeat and an ultrasound to check fluid levels, along with a conversation about next steps.

Waiting well, and when to go in

There is no proven, reliably safe home method to start labor, which is worth knowing before you buy anything. Walking, staying gently active, and sex when your water has not broken are reasonable and pleasant, even though the evidence for all of them is mixed. Skip castor oil and unverified herbal preparations unless your clinician specifically recommends them, since they can cause strong cramping and dehydration. Spend the energy on rest instead: sleep when you can, keep meals simple, install the car seat, pack the bag, and confirm exactly who you will call first when contractions start, day or night.

Call your maternity unit or go in if your water breaks, if you have bright red bleeding, if contractions become regular and strong following the pattern your provider gave you, often about five minutes apart and lasting a minute each for an hour with a first baby, or if your baby's movements decrease. A severe headache that will not ease, vision changes, or sudden swelling of your face and hands need an immediate call, whatever the hour, because they can signal preeclampsia. Our signs of labor guide covers true versus false labor in more detail. Jotting contraction times and questions in BeMama or on paper keeps the details handy for that first phone call, and once the bag is packed, a simple postpartum plan is the natural next thing to sketch.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and is commonly described in weeks and trimesters. ACOG’s week ranges describe typical development, but they are an orientation rather than a test of an individual fetus.

Due dates are estimates, and ultrasound is used for medical reasons to assess gestational age, growth, anatomy, position, and other questions. Only a qualified prenatal professional can interpret findings for a specific pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s week view for education, appointment preparation, and dated notes. It cannot confirm fetal growth, anatomy, heartbeat, or wellbeing.

When to seek help

Contact your prenatal team for bleeding, severe pain, fluid leakage, reduced movement after movement is established, or any urgent concern instead of relying on a week-by-week article.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — How Your Fetus Grows During Pregnancy
  • ACOG — Ultrasound Exams
  • CDC — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Full term begins at 39 weeks 0 days; 37 to 38 weeks 6 days counts as early term.
  • Most babies arrive around 48 to 52 cm long and 3 to 3.6 kg, and are mainly gaining fat now.
  • Weekly visits continue, and cervical checks and membrane sweeps are optional choices, not requirements.
  • Going past your due date is common; closer monitoring and induction talks usually start around 41 weeks.
  • Go in for broken waters, bleeding, regular strong contractions, or reduced movement.

Frequently asked questions

Is 37 weeks full term?

No, 37 weeks is early term; full term begins at 39 weeks 0 days under the definitions used by ACOG. Babies born at 37 to 38 weeks usually do well, but those extra days of lung and brain maturing are why elective deliveries are generally not scheduled before 39 weeks. If labor starts on its own at 37 weeks, your team will simply care for the birth as usual.

I am 40 weeks pregnant with no signs of labor. Is that normal?

Yes, reaching 40 weeks with no signs of labor is common, especially with a first baby, and it does not mean anything is wrong. Due dates are estimates, and many labors begin in the week after them. Your clinician will usually add extra monitoring, such as a nonstress test, and discuss options like a membrane sweep or induction if you approach 41 to 42 weeks.

What is a membrane sweep?

A membrane sweep is a procedure where a clinician sweeps a gloved finger around the inside of the cervix during a vaginal exam to separate the amniotic sac membranes from the cervix. This releases natural prostaglandins and can help labor start within a few days, though it does not always work. It can be uncomfortable and cause spotting and cramping, and it is always optional.

When should I go to the hospital for labor?

Go in, or call your maternity unit first, when contractions are regular and strong per the guideline your provider gave you, commonly around five minutes apart and lasting about a minute for an hour with a first baby. Go without waiting if your water breaks, if you are bleeding, or if your baby is moving less than usual. When in doubt, call: triage lines expect these questions at every hour of the night.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
